clinicalPearls: Historically defined by an elevated resting lower oesophageal sphincter pressure with otherwise normal deglutitive relaxation and preserved oesophageal body peristalsis.

In the modern Chicago Classification the isolated finding is no longer a stand-alone diagnosis; the key clinical question is whether relaxation is normal or whether the picture actually represents oesophagogastric junction outflow obstruction or early achalasia.
Symptoms, when present, are dysphagia and chest pain, but the finding is frequently incidental and of uncertain clinical significance in an asymptomatic patient.
Normal integrated relaxation pressure argues against a true outflow-obstructing disorder and supports a benign interpretation of the elevated basal tone.
Coexisting gastro-oesophageal reflux and oesophageal hypersensitivity should be evaluated as alternative explanations for symptoms.
Management is directed by symptoms: reassurance where mild, smooth-muscle relaxants and neuromodulators for troublesome chest pain or dysphagia.
Botulinum toxin injection into the sphincter may be tried in refractory symptomatic cases, with pneumatic dilatation or myotomy reserved for those reclassified as outflow obstruction or achalasia.
Because isolated sphincter hypertension can be an early or evolving stage of an outflow disorder, follow-up assessment is prudent when symptoms persist or worsen.
reference.pathophysiology: Hypertensive lower oesophageal sphincter denotes an abnormally elevated resting tone of the sphincter in the setting of preserved swallow-induced relaxation and normal oesophageal body peristalsis. The mechanism is incompletely understood but is thought to reflect an imbalance between excitatory cholinergic tone and inhibitory nitrergic input at the sphincter, producing sustained hypertonicity without the failure of relaxation that characterises achalasia. When relaxation becomes impaired, the disorder is better classified as oesophagogastric junction outflow obstruction, and some patients with sphincter hypertension progress along this spectrum toward achalasia. Symptom generation, particularly chest pain, is amplified by oesophageal hypersensitivity, which accounts for the weak correlation between the manometric abnormality and clinical severity.
additionalDifferentials: functional chest pain and oesophageal hypersensitivity
mechanical obstruction at the oesophagogastric junction (stricture, tumour, tight fundoplication)
additionalInvestigations: high-resolution oesophageal manometry with integrated relaxation pressure measurement
upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to exclude mechanical obstruction and mucosal disease
timed barium oesophagram to assess emptying
functional lumen imaging probe (FLIP) to characterise oesophagogastric junction distensibility
provocative manometric manoeuvres (rapid drink challenge, solid swallows)
cardiac assessment when chest pain is prominent
redFlags: progressive dysphagia or weight loss suggesting evolving achalasia or malignancy
impaired oesophagogastric junction relaxation on manometry indicating an outflow-obstructing disorder
endoscopic resistance at the oesophagogastric junction or a mass lesion
reference.prognosis: The isolated finding is generally benign and may be asymptomatic or respond to conservative measures; however, a proportion of patients evolve toward oesophagogastric junction outflow obstruction or achalasia, warranting surveillance when symptoms persist. Prognosis in the latter groups follows that of the reclassified disorder.
pitfalls: Treating an incidental elevated sphincter pressure in an asymptomatic patient.
Failing to measure and interpret the integrated relaxation pressure, thereby missing true outflow obstruction or achalasia.
Not excluding a mechanical cause such as a tumour or overly tight fundoplication at the oesophagogastric junction.
Overlooking reflux and hypersensitivity as the actual source of chest pain.
Assuming the finding is static and omitting follow-up when symptoms progress.

management: Reassurance and conservative management where the finding is mild, incidental or asymptomatic
Smooth-muscle relaxants such as calcium-channel blockers or nitrates for troublesome dysphagia or chest pain
Neuromodulators such as low-dose tricyclic antidepressants to address oesophageal hypersensitivity-driven chest pain
Treat coexisting gastro-oesophageal reflux with a proton pump inhibitor as an alternative explanation for symptoms
If the picture evolves into oesophagogastric junction outflow obstruction or achalasia, consider botulinum toxin injection, pneumatic dilatation or myotomy
Surveillance with repeat high-resolution manometry when symptoms persist or progress
